Compared with the prior excerpt, the full July 27, 2022 FOMC statement tilts clearly hawkish: despite acknowledging softer spending and production, it stresses robust job gains, elevated inflation, and “ongoing increases” in the policy rate alongside balance-sheet runoff. Literature on inflation-at-risk (2024) shows that when the distribution of inflation is skewed to the upside—typical under energy shocks related to the Russia–Ukraine war—policymakers optimally lean more aggressively against inflation risk; this supports the Committee’s “highly attentive to inflation risks” language and hawkish guidance. Pandemic-era research on shifting consumption baskets and measurement (e.g., COVID-19 Inflation Weighting in Israel, 2022) and evidence of broader price pressures and markups (The Beginning of the Trend: Interest Rates, Profits and Markups, 2023) both imply inflation persistence beyond food/energy, reinforcing a tighter stance even as growth slows. Finally, Taylor-rule estimates and policy-inertia evidence (Papell, Molodtsova, and Nikolsko-Rzhevskyy, 2008) suggest that with high inflation and low unemployment, the rule-prescribed rate exceeds neutral, consistent with the 75 bp hike and guidance for further increases. Net tone: distinctly hawkish with a nod to growth risks.
